chunks.text: 2.1 Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting with Coupled Architectures Most existing deep learning approaches for traffic forecasting adopt coupled spatio-temporal modeling strategies Jiang et al. (2023b) ; Yu et al. (2018) ; Li and Zhu (2021) , where spatial interaction learning and temporal dependency modeling are tightly intertwined. Early models such as STGCN Yu et al. (2018) combine graph convolution with temporal convolution to capture localized spatial-temporal dependencies, while DCRNN Li et al. (2018) models traffic diffusion on directed graphs using recurrent encoder-decoder structures. Graph WaveNet Wu et al. (2019) further improves this line by introducing an adaptive dependency matrix to capture hidden spatial relations beyond predefined road connectivity. More recent transformer-style architectures further strengthen this coupling by using spatio-temporal attention to dynamically model interactions across nodes and time steps Zheng et al. (2019) ; Wang et al. (2024) ; Jiang et al. (2023a) . ASTGCN Guo et al. (2019) leverages spatial and temporal attention to identify important nodes and time intervals. STFGNN Li and Zhu (2021) builds a spatial-temporal fusion graph to capture correlations across nodes and time steps. AGCRN Bai et al. (2020) and MTGNN Wu et al. (2020) learn adaptive graph structures for end-to-end spatial-temporal forecasting. Transformer-based models, such as GMAN Zheng et al. (2019) , STAEformer Liu et al. (2023) , PDFormer Jiang et al. (2023a) , and STGformer Wang et al. (2024) , further improve long-range dependency modeling through spatial-temporal attention, adaptive embeddings, propagation-aware mechanisms, and efficient graph transformer designs. These models demonstrate strong predictive accuracy on large-scale benchmarks, particularly when long-range spatial and temporal dependencies are prominent. However, their performance often comes at the cost of increased architectural complexity and computational overhead.

More importantly, the repeated interleaving of spatial interaction learning and temporal modeling reduces modularity: spatial and temporal components are difficult to isolate, reuse, or simplify, which can hinder flexible deployment when forecasting models are used as standalone modules in larger systems. Figure 1 : The architecture of the proposed UniST-Pred model. 2.2 Decoupled Perspectives: Efficient Temporal Modeling and Task-Adaptive Spatial Encoding Recent studies have explored more modular or decoupled learning strategies for traffic forecasting. ST-SSL Ji et al. (2023) improves spatial-temporal representations through self-supervised objectives, partially separating representation learning from the final supervised forecasting task. Along this direction, STEP Shao et al. (2022) and STD-MAE Gao et al. (2024) further demonstrate the value of pre-training-based representation learning. STEP adopts a pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm to learn transferable spatial-temporal knowledge before adapting it to downstream forecasting tasks. STD-MAE extends this perspective by explicitly decoupling spatial and temporal dependency learning within a masked pre-training framework. Together, these methods illustrate that separating representation acquisition from task-specific prediction can improve transferability and robustness in spatial-temporal forecasting. In parallel, the time-series forecasting community has shown that long-range temporal dependencies can be modeled efficiently without heavy recurrent or attention-based sequence modeling. Mixer-style architectures Chen et al. (2023) and efficient transformer variants Nie et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024) demonstrate that temporal dependency learning can be decomposed into simple operations along the time and feature dimensions, achieving competitive performance with significantly reduced complexity.

These results suggest that expressive temporal modeling does not inherently require tight coupling with spatial interaction mechanisms. Separately, another line of research questions the reliance on fixed graph structures for spatial modeling. Graph structure learning and relation composition methods argue that a single predefined adjacency matrix may be suboptimal for downstream tasks. Graph Transformer Networks Yun et al. (2019) exemplify this perspective by learning task-adaptive graph structures through soft composition of candidate relations. In traffic forecasting, related ideas appear in models that infer dynamic or attention-based spatial dependencies rather than relying solely on physical road connectivity. 4 Methodology We propose a unified spatio-temporal framework for traffic forecasting under dynamic scenarios where network topology may change (e.g., road closures). The model decouples temporal modeling and spatial representation learning, then integrates them via an adaptive fusion module (Fig. 1 ). For temporal dependencies, we adopt feature/time mixing Chen et al. (2023) to capture long-range dynamics efficiently, and for spatial dependencies we employ graph-based encoding to leverage road-network structure without assuming a fixed topology. This separation-and-fusion design improves robustness to evolving connectivity and heterogeneous traffic conditions. Temporal Modeling via Feature and Time Mixing: The temporal block models long-range dependencies and cross-feature interactions using feature/time mixing instead of RNNs or attention. This design captures both short-term variations and long-term patterns efficiently. The time and feature mixing layer is stated as below: (a) Mixer operators. We use ℳ \mathcal{M} to denote structured mixing operators applied to tensor representations.

Specifically, ℳ time \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{time}} denotes a time-mixing operator that acts along the temporal dimension independently for each node and feature, while ℳ feat \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{feat}} denotes a feature-mixing operator that models cross-channel interactions at each time step. Both operators preserve the input shape and are implemented as learnable linear-nonlinear transformations. (b) Stacked temporal operator. The temporal modeling function is defined as a composition of K K stacked temporal mixer blocks: f temp := 𝒯 ( K ) θ K ∘ 𝒯 ( K − 1 ) θ K − 1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ 𝒯 ( 1 ) θ 1 f_{\mathrm{temp}}:=\mathcal{T}^{(K)}_{\theta_{K}}\circ\mathcal{T}^{(K-1)}_{\theta_{K-1}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{T}^{(1)}_{\theta_{1}} , where each temporal mixer block 𝒯 θ k ( k ) \mathcal{T}^{(k)}_{\theta_{k}} is given by 𝒯 ( k ) θ k = ℳ ( k ) feat ∘ ℳ ( k ) time , k = 1 , … , K . \mathcal{T}^{(k)}_{\theta_{k}}=\mathcal{M}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{feat}}\circ\mathcal{M}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{time}},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K. (1) Given an input sequence 𝐗 t − H + 1 : t \mathbf{X}_{t-H+1:t} , the temporal representation is computed as 𝐘 1 = f temp ( 𝐗 t − H + 1 : t ) = ( ○ k = 1 K ℳ ( k ) feat ∘ ℳ ( k ) time ) ( 𝐗 t − H + 1 : t ) . \begin{split}\mathbf{Y}_{1}=&f_{\mathrm{temp}}(\mathbf{X}_{t-H+1:t})=\\ &\left(\bigcirc_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{M}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{feat}}\circ\mathcal{M}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{time}}\right)\left(\mathbf{X}_{t-H+1:t}\right).\end{split} (2) Here, ∘ \circ denotes function composition, and ○ k = 1 K \bigcirc_{k=1}^{K} denotes ordered composition from block 1 1 to K K , with each block applying time-mixing followed by feature-mixing. By avoiding sequential inductive biases, the temporal module provides a flexible representation of traffic dynamics that generalizes across traffic regimes and temporal resolutions. The resulting temporal embeddings focus on intrinsic time-series characteristics, independent of spatial structure.

Spatial Representation Learning with Graph-Based Encoding: The spatial block uses the road network as structural context to extract spatial features. Rather than relying on inductive message passing, it learns which road connections are most relevant to the task. Following a GTN-style approach, the model constructs task-adaptive graph structures by softly masking road segments, combining candidate relations, and applying lightweight graph convolutions. This lightweight design produces effective spatial embeddings that capture essential structural patterns and remain robust to partial topology changes. Adaptive Fusion via Squeeze-Excitation Residual Integration: To jointly exploit temporal and spatial information, the proposed framework integrates the two representations through a squeeze–excitation Hu et al. (2018) residual fusion block, which adaptively reweights temporal and spatial features based on their relative importance. Given the temporal representation 𝐘 1 = f temp ( 𝐗 t − H + 1 : t ) , \mathbf{Y}_{1}=f_{\mathrm{temp}}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_{t-H+1:t}\right), and the spatial representation 𝐘 2 = f spat ​ ( 𝐗 ′ ) , \mathbf{Y}_{2}=f_{\mathrm{spat}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}), we first stack the two representations to form a joint feature: 𝐘 = Stack ⁡ ( 𝐘 1 , 𝐘 2 ) . \mathbf{Y}=\mathrm{Stack}(\mathbf{Y}_{1},\mathbf{Y}_{2}). By performing fusion at the representation level rather than tightly coupling spatio-temporal propagation, the framework maintains modularity and interpretability. The residual connection further ensures stable gradient flow and preserves strong temporal representations while incorporating spatial cues, leading to robust and adaptive traffic forecasting across diverse scenarios. The time and feature mixing layer is stated as below: 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup & Settings Datasets: We evaluate our method on three different datasets: • SimSF-Bay : SimSF-Bay, introduced in this work, is a traffic flow dataset derived from MATSim simulations of the SF Bay area’s transportation network. The underlying MATSim model and its configurations were adopted from Papakonstantinou et al. (2020) . The network comprises 7,709 road segments, with traffic flow recorded at 5-minute intervals. The traffic flow from the previous 45 minutes is used as input for predicting the next time step (prediction horizon H ′ = 1 H^{\prime}=1 ). • PEMS-Bay Li et al. (2018) : PEMS-Bay is a traffic speed dataset collected from the California Transportation Agencies (CalTrans) Performance Measurement System (PeMS) for the Bay Area. It contains data from 325 sensors over a 6-month period, from January 1, 2017 to May 31, 2017. Traffic information is recorded at 5-minute intervals.

Traffic data from the previous 7 days around the predicted time are used to forecast the next 12 time steps (prediction horizon H ′ = 12 H^{\prime}=12 ). • NYCTaxi Zheng et al. (2014) : NYCTaxi is a taxi trajectory dataset for New York City, spanning from January 1, 2015 to March 1, 2015. The data are recorded at 30-minute intervals. Traffic flow from the previous 17.5 hours is used to forecast the flow for the next time step (prediction horizon H ′ = 1 H^{\prime}=1 ). The PEMS-Bay and NYCTaxi datasets follow the standard setting and assume a fixed transportation network or spatial discretization, with traffic states evolving over time. In contrast, SimSF-Bay captures scenario-dependent topological variations, including changes in network connectivity and link availability, while maintaining a fixed simulation horizon consistent with standard agent-based transport modeling practice. This setting enables the assessment of model robustness under structural network changes, which is not supported by existing benchmarks. Additional details on the datasets are provided in Sec. B . Baselines & Metrics: We compare our method against a diverse set of established time series forecasting approaches, covering classical statistical models, temporal deep learning methods, and spatio-temporal graph neural networks. Specifically, the baselines include ARIMA Kumar and Vanajakshi (2015) , LSTM Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) , TCN Lea et al. (2017) , TSMixer and its extended variant TSMixer-ext Chen et al. (2023) , as well as several spatio-temporal models, including STGCN Yu et al. (2018) , ASTGCN Guo et al. (2019) , ST-SSL Ji et al. (2023) , DCRNN Li et al. (2018) , and STEP Shao et al. (2022) .

For evaluation, we follow standard practice and report RMSE, MAE, and MAPE, formally defined as follows: RMSE = 1 N ​ ∑ t = 1 N ( y t − y ^ t ) 2 , MAE = 1 N ∑ t = 1 N | y t − y ^ t | , MAPE = 1 N ​ ∑ t = 1 N | y t − y ^ t y t | × 100 % , \begin{split}&\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}\right)^{2}},\quad\mathrm{MAE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left|y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}\right|,\\ &\mathrm{MAPE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left|\frac{y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}}{y_{t}}\right|\times 100\%,\end{split} where { y ^ i } i = 1 N \{\hat{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and { y i } i = 1 N \{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the predictions and the ground truth values, respectively. It is noted that for MAPE calculation a mask was applied on the raw ground truth values to filter out zero and near-zero values. Reproducibility: The source code, dataset, and evaluation scripts associated with this work are publicly available in our project repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/yw3576/UniST-Pred . 5.2 Performance Comparison Quantitative Evaluation: Table 1 reports the quantitative comparison results. On SimSF-Bay, UniST-Pred consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving the lowest errors across all evaluation metrics, while TS-Mixer achieves the second best RMSE. On PEMS-Bay, UniST-Pred performs on par with the strongest baseline, STEP, in terms of RMSE, and remains close to the best MAE (1.91 versus 1.79 for STEP). This indicates that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the leading baseline on this dataset, while its MAPE remains competitive, though lagging behind STEP. On NYC-Taxi, UniST-Pred achieves the lowest RMSE and MAE, with noticeable margins over the closest baseline. Again, TS-Mixer achieves the second best RMSE, while STEP attains better MAPE, with UniST-Pred ranking second. Taken together, these results indicate that UniST-Pred consistently captures absolute error patterns, as reflected by having best results in RMSE and MAE across datasets.

While average accuracy reflects overall performance, it does not show whether gains are consistent across locations or driven by a subset of easy cases. To examine spatial error patterns, Fig. 2 reports per-location MAPE distributions for TSMixer, STEP, and UniST-Pred across all datasets. Locations are divided by traffic flow percentiles, with high flow locations in the top 25% and low flow locations in the lower 75%. Each stacked bar shows the proportion of locations with low (0–33%), medium (33–66%), or high (66–100%) MAPE. Figure 2 : Per-location MAPE distribution for UniST-Pred, STEP, and TSMixer on three datasets, stratified by high and low traffic flow. (Light colors indicate lower error.) On SimSF-Bay, UniST-Pred achieves lower error on more locations than STEP and TSMixer, for both high-flow and low-flow locations. On PEMS-Bay and NYCTaxi, STEP shows a clear advantage on low-flow locations, while UniST-Pred matches or outperforms STEP on high-flow locations. These results suggest that UniST-Pred performs particularly well on high-traffic locations, which are often the most operationally important for traffic management applications. Qualitative Evaluation: To examine prediction quality, Fig. 3 shows the ground truth and predictions over all roads for three datasets, comparing UniST-Pred with STEP and TSMixer on a representative sample period. For SimSF-Bay, all methods capture the main periodic pattern. In PEMS-Bay, UniST-Pred tracks the broad pattern of the averaged speed and preserves the overall level and long-range trend, whereas STEP and TSMixer exhibit larger deviations near abrupt local changes. For NYCTaxi, all methods closely follow the ground truth across cycles, with UniST-Pred showing slightly higher fidelity, while the other methods exhibit slightly increased smoothing or variability.

These results suggest that UniST-Pred (i) captures dominant temporal dynamics with better phase alignment, (ii) maintains stable predictions without noticeable drift over long horizons, and (iii) provides smooth and consistent estimates of the global signal, which is beneficial when the objective is accurate trend-level forecasting on network-aggregated traffic patterns. Figure 3 : Qualitative comparison of ground truth and model predictions. Model Size: Next, we compare the number of model parameters of UniST-Pred against STEP, one of the strongest baseline methods. As shown in Table 2 , UniST-Pred is substantially more parameter efficient than STEP across all three datasets. This reduction is particularly noticeable on SimSF-Bay and PEMS-Bay, where our model is approximately 4.0 × \times and 3.7 × \times smaller than STEP, respectively, and becomes especially significant on NYC-Taxi, where UniST-Pred is over 30 × \times smaller. This consistent reduction indicates that the proposed architecture achieves a favorable accuracy to efficiency trade-off, making it more suitable for deployment under computational constraints while maintaining strong predictive performance. To analyze the contribution of individual components in the proposed architecture, we conduct an ablation study by systematically removing or replacing key sub-modules. Specifically, we consider variants that remove the spatial block, the temporal block, or the fusion block, as well as variants that replace the spatial block with standard GCN layers or the temporal block with a fully connected (FC) layers. Table 4 presents the ablation study results. We observe that removing either the spatial block or the temporal block consistently degrades performance across all metrics. Similarly, replacing the spatial block with standard GCN layers or the temporal block with fully connected layers increases the error. The w/o fusion variant performs competitively among simplified settings, indicating that the backbone alone can learn informative representations. The full model achieves the lowest error across all metrics, confirming that all proposed components contribute to the best overall performance.

Darker color indicates higher contribution to the prediction. We conclude the empirical evaluation by examining the robustness of UniST-Pred under major infrastructure disruptions. To this end, we use the adopted MATSim model to construct six stress-test scenarios on the SF Bay Area network by removing major bridges or freeway/highway links that play a critical role in the region’s connectivity. Specifically, we consider the removal/closing of (Scenario 1) Oakland Bay Bridge; (Scenario 2) Carquinez Bridge and San Rafael Bridge; (Scenario 3) Golden Gate Bridge and Dumbarton Bridge; (Scenario 4) US-101 highway (near Brisbane); (Scenario 5) the shared segment of I-80 and I-580 freeways near Albany; and (Scenario 6) the links considered in Scenarios 4 and 5. Robustness Under Disruption: Fig. 4 compares the ground truth traffic flow and the predictions produced by UniST-Pred, both at the level of the network-wide average and for two representative roads, across all six scenarios. At the aggregate level (top row), the predictions closely track the ground truth. For individual roads (middle and bottom rows), the predictions remain trend-consistent, though brief local spikes may be smoothed or missed.

A quantitative comparison against TSMixer and STEP is reported in Table 5 , which shows that UniST-Pred attains the lowest RMSE in all six disruption scenarios as well as in the fully connected setting, indicating consistently strong performance across different connectivity conditions. Explainability Analysis: Complementary to the above, we study the attribution behavior of UniST-Pred under disruption scenarios by examining which road segments contribute most to its predictions. To this end, we first leverage the trained UniST-Pred model to generate traffic predictions, then apply Integrated Gradients (IG), which quantifies the contribution of each input feature by integrating gradients along a straight-line path from a baseline 𝐱 ′ \mathbf{x}^{\prime} to the input 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . More concretely, for a differentiable scalar output F ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) F(\mathbf{x}) , the IG attribution for feature i i is calculated as IG i ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ( x i − x i ′ ) ​ ∫ 0 1 ∂ F ⁡ ( 𝐱 ′ + α ⁡ ( 𝐱 − 𝐱 ′ ) ) ∂ x i ​ 𝑑 α . \mathrm{IG}_{i}(\mathbf{x})=(x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i})\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\partial F\big(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}+\alpha(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\big)}{\partial x_{i}}\,d\alpha. Fig. 5 visualizes the resulting road-level IG contribution maps, where darker segments correspond to higher contribution to the model’s prediction. The figure contrasts the fully connected network (middle panel) with the disrupted cases in Scenario 1 and Scenario 4 (right panels), revealing a clear redistribution of attribution under disruption.

For evaluation, we follow standard practice and report RMSE, MAE, and MAPE, formally defined as follows: RMSE = 1 N ​ ∑ t = 1 N ( y t − y ^ t ) 2 , MAE = 1 N ∑ t = 1 N | y t − y ^ t | , MAPE = 1 N ​ ∑ t = 1 N | y t − y ^ t y t | × 100 % , \begin{split}&\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}\right)^{2}},\quad\mathrm{MAE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left|y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}\right|,\\ &\mathrm{MAPE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left|\frac{y_{t}-\hat{y}_{t}}{y_{t}}\right|\times 100\%,\end{split} where { y ^ i } i = 1 N \{\hat{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and { y i } i = 1 N \{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the predictions and the ground truth values, respectively. It is noted that for MAPE calculation a mask was applied on the raw ground truth values to filter out zero and near-zero values.

Reproducibility: The source code, dataset, and evaluation scripts associated with this work are publicly available in our project repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/yw3576/UniST-Pred . Datasets: We evaluate our method on three different datasets: • SimSF-Bay : SimSF-Bay, introduced in this work, is a traffic flow dataset derived from MATSim simulations of the SF Bay area’s transportation network. The underlying MATSim model and its configurations were adopted from Papakonstantinou et al. (2020) . The network comprises 7,709 road segments, with traffic flow recorded at 5-minute intervals. The traffic flow from the previous 45 minutes is used as input for predicting the next time step (prediction horizon H ′ = 1 H^{\prime}=1 ). • PEMS-Bay Li et al. (2018) : PEMS-Bay is a traffic speed dataset collected from the California Transportation Agencies (CalTrans) Performance Measurement System (PeMS) for the Bay Area. It contains data from 325 sensors over a 6-month period, from January 1, 2017 to May 31, 2017. Traffic information is recorded at 5-minute intervals. Traffic data from the previous 7 days around the predicted time are used to forecast the next 12 time steps (prediction horizon H ′ = 12 H^{\prime}=12 ). • NYCTaxi Zheng et al. (2014) : NYCTaxi is a taxi trajectory dataset for New York City, spanning from January 1, 2015 to March 1, 2015. The data are recorded at 30-minute intervals. Traffic flow from the previous 17.5 hours is used to forecast the flow for the next time step (prediction horizon H ′ = 1 H^{\prime}=1 ). The PEMS-Bay and NYCTaxi datasets follow the standard setting and assume a fixed transportation network or spatial discretization, with traffic states evolving over time. In contrast, SimSF-Bay captures scenario-dependent topological variations, including changes in network connectivity and link availability, while maintaining a fixed simulation horizon consistent with standard agent-based transport modeling practice.

This setting enables the assessment of model robustness under structural network changes, which is not supported by existing benchmarks. Additional details on the datasets are provided in Sec. B . Quantitative Evaluation: Table 1 reports the quantitative comparison results. On SimSF-Bay, UniST-Pred consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving the lowest errors across all evaluation metrics, while TS-Mixer achieves the second best RMSE. On PEMS-Bay, UniST-Pred performs on par with the strongest baseline, STEP, in terms of RMSE, and remains close to the best MAE (1.91 versus 1.79 for STEP). This indicates that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the leading baseline on this dataset, while its MAPE remains competitive, though lagging behind STEP. On NYC-Taxi, UniST-Pred achieves the lowest RMSE and MAE, with noticeable margins over the closest baseline. Again, TS-Mixer achieves the second best RMSE, while STEP attains better MAPE, with UniST-Pred ranking second. Taken together, these results indicate that UniST-Pred consistently captures absolute error patterns, as reflected by having best results in RMSE and MAE across datasets. While average accuracy reflects overall performance, it does not show whether gains are consistent across locations or driven by a subset of easy cases. Qualitative Evaluation: To examine prediction quality, Fig. 3 shows the ground truth and predictions over all roads for three datasets, comparing UniST-Pred with STEP and TSMixer on a representative sample period. For SimSF-Bay, all methods capture the main periodic pattern. In PEMS-Bay, UniST-Pred tracks the broad pattern of the averaged speed and preserves the overall level and long-range trend, whereas STEP and TSMixer exhibit larger deviations near abrupt local changes. For NYCTaxi, all methods closely follow the ground truth across cycles, with UniST-Pred showing slightly higher fidelity, while the other methods exhibit slightly increased smoothing or variability. These results suggest that UniST-Pred (i) captures dominant temporal dynamics with better phase alignment, (ii) maintains stable predictions without noticeable drift over long horizons, and (iii) provides smooth and consistent estimates of the global signal, which is beneficial when the objective is accurate trend-level forecasting on network-aggregated traffic patterns. To analyze the contribution of individual components in the proposed architecture, we conduct an ablation study by systematically removing or replacing key sub-modules. Specifically, we consider variants that remove the spatial block, the temporal block, or the fusion block, as well as variants that replace the spatial block with standard GCN layers or the temporal block with a fully connected (FC) layers. Table 4 presents the ablation study results. We observe that removing either the spatial block or the temporal block consistently degrades performance across all metrics. Similarly, replacing the spatial block with standard GCN layers or the temporal block with fully connected layers increases the error. The w/o fusion variant performs competitively among simplified settings, indicating that the backbone alone can learn informative representations.

The full model achieves the lowest error across all metrics, confirming that all proposed components contribute to the best overall performance. 6 Conclusion This work studies spatio-temporal traffic forecasting as a modular modeling problem and proposes a unified framework that decouples temporal dependency learning from spatial representation extraction with adaptive fusion. By avoiding tightly coupled spatio-temporal propagation, the framework provides a lightweight yet expressive alternative for traffic prediction. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that the proposed design achieves competitive performance with a compact architecture, while additional analyses offer insights into the contributions of temporal and spatial components. More broadly, this study suggests that a decouple-then-fuse strategy can serve as a useful design principle for spatio-temporal learning, with relevance beyond traffic forecasting and practical importance for real world traffic networks. Appendix A MATSim Simulator & SF Bay Transportation Network Model MATSim (Multi-Agent Transport Simulation) W Axhausen et al. (2016) is a microscopic, agent-based transportation simulator widely utilized in transportation planning and mobility research. MATSim models travel demand explicitly at the individual level, representing each traveler as an autonomous agent with daily activity plans that evolve through iterative re-planning and network loading. At each iteration, agents execute their plans on a detailed transportation network, generating time-resolved link-level traffic states such as flow, speed, and travel time, which are subsequently used to update agent plans based on experienced costs and utilities defined by user-assigned scoring functions. The simulation is considered converged once agents’ plans and experienced costs stabilize across successive iterations, corresponding to a stochastic user equilibrium.

Owing to its realism and flexibility, MATSim is commonly employed by academic researchers, transportation authorities, and planning agencies for scenario analysis, policy evaluation, and infrastructure planning. Within the scope of current study, we adopt from Papakonstantinou et al. (2020) the MATSim model calibrated for the San Francisco Bay Area. In this model, the commuters travel plan is based on the vehicular travel information from Pozdnoukhov et al. Pozdnoukhov et al. (2016) . The demand model is based on anonymised cellular network infrastructure data stream and census data from the 2010-2012 California Household Travel Survey data. The demand generation relies on the 1454 Traffic Analysis Zones in the area developed by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (see https://abag.ca.gov/sites/default/files/pba_2050-regional_growth_forecast_methodology.pdf ). The model considers a sample population of 463,938 commuters and the road links in the transportation network are scaled down to 8% of their original capacities to correctly match the population scale.
